items.q: He played a few numbers with us

ctx.x: Now and then, musicians would drop by the Capitol to listen to the band and some would sit in for some jam sessions. One that I had not heard about was a trumpeter named Cuban Bennett. This man was a musician's musician because he had a style in the order of Joe Smith but he did more changes, as harmony was called, and he did not use a plunger like Joe Smith did. I mean that his tone was like Joe's because it was mellow and round. He played a few numbers with us and then he asked Don Frye if he knew "Fascinating…
Cuban was a cousin of Benny Carter but I was told that he was an alcoholic and no one could rely on him. He could have been in some of the best

orchestras in the city I was told, but if he was hired by anyone they knew the chance they were taking. He was a swell person to know and more than a wonderful musician. The only harm he ever did to anyone was to himself. Of course he was not the only musician that alcohol would not let go anywhere, but it was a pity that this happened to such a talented man as Cuban Bennett.

items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Cuban Bennett used to make this place his second home and that's where I really became acquainted with his style of trumpet.

ctx.x: I met a fellow about my age named Bob Sawyer who became a good friend of mine. The first new friend I had made in New York. The dancers that were regular customers and top "Lindy Hoppers" became our friends also. There were such names as Shorty, Twisted-Mouth George, the Sheik, Slim Willy and Fats Rolland. They and the girls they danced with were our real supporters but Bob became a real friend of mine. He showed me how to tie a bow tie. I bought them already tied before that.
